say.en: The tallest redwoods are over 110 metres high. No suction pump can lift water more than about 10 metres, yet these trees supply their highest leaves every day. In this lesson: Trace the path of water from the soil to the xylem.
Describe root pressure.
Explain the cohesion-tension-transpiration pull theory.

title.en: From the soil to the xylem

body.en: Root hairs take up water mainly by osmosis. In the cortex, water moves by the apoplast (cell walls and spaces, no membranes crossed) and the symplast (cytoplasm linked by plasmodesmata). At the endodermis the suberised Casparian strip blocks the apoplast, so water and minerals must pass through living cells, which can control the minerals. Water then enters the *xylem*. Active loading of ions into the xylem draws water in and builds a small positive root pressure, seen as guttation and sap oozing from cut stems.

points.en: Apoplast: walls and spaces; symplast: cytoplasm
Casparian strip forces *water* into the symplast
*Root pressure* pushes water up only a few metres

body.en: Most water is pulled, not pushed. Water evaporates from the walls of mesophyll cells and leaves through stomata. This makes a tension (negative pressure) that is passed down the continuous column of water in the xylem. The column does not break because water molecules attract each other (cohesion), stick to the xylem walls (adhesion) and the narrow tubes give high surface tension. Thus *transpiration pulls* water all the way from the roots.

heading.en: Water Absorption, Ascent of Sap and Transpiration

tagline.en: How roots absorb water through the apoplast and symplast, root pressure and guttation, the cohesion–tension–transpiration pull model, stomatal opening, factors affecting transpiration and its uses to the plant.

myth.en: Root pressure pushes water to the top of tall trees.

truth.en: The main force in tall trees is the transpiration pull; root pressure gives only a modest push. Root pressure is easy to see as oozing sap, so it seems powerful. It is absent or low in many trees and cannot support columns tens of metres tall.

say.en: Apoplast: walls and spaces, fast, blocked by the Casparian strip; symplast: through cytoplasm and plasmodesmata.
Root pressure: active ion uptake into xylem; seen as exudation and guttation; minor in tall trees.
Cohesion, adhesion and surface tension let transpiration pull water up the xylem.
Stomata open when guard cells are turgid; radial microfibrils help; transpiration cools leaves and carries minerals.

problem.en: A water column must be pulled up a 50 m tree. Gravity alone needs about 0.01 MPa per metre, and friction in the xylem roughly doubles it. Estimate the tension needed. Could root pressure (0.2 MPa) do it?

answer.en: About 1 MPa; root pressure is not enough

prompt.en: Put the path of water through a plant in order.

steps.en: Soil water enters the root hair by osmosis.
It crosses the cortex by the apoplast and symplast.
It passes through the endodermal cells (Casparian strip).
It enters the xylem of the root.
It rises in the xylem of the stem as a cohesive column.
It reaches the mesophyll cells of the leaf.
It evaporates and leaves through the stomata.
